note: Guide check: section 4.4, pp.30-31. Requirements describe the features needed to satisfy stakeholders' needs. If requestor and provider are both certain the requirements specification describes the solution completely, the traditional upfront planning approach can be used. When the requirements are not entirely known, or the rate of change is high, agile and Lean UX approaches yield better results. The guide also warns that requirements derived from a known solution express the 'how' rather than the 'what'. The first step is to clarify the problem to be solved, and the guide is explicit that the problem or need should be fully documented in the PM² Business Case before requirements are gathered. Nothing here is a PM²-Agile project yet: no Project Initiation Request, therefore no Project Owner, no Product Owner, no Work Items List. RASCI row: none. Approver: none, because nothing exists to approve. Pages 30-31.
notePlain: Rule: requirements describe what people need. If both sides are sure a written specification describes the whole solution, use the normal PM² way. When the requirements are not really known, or they change often, agile and Lean UX work better (page 30). The guide also warns that people often describe a solution they have already imagined. That is the 'how', not the 'what'. So the first job is to make the problem clear, and the guide says to write that problem fully in the Business Case before collecting requirements (page 31). Here there is no project yet, so there are no roles, no Work Items List and nobody to approve anything. Pages 30 and 31.

options.why: PM²-Agile does not replace any part of PM² (p.2). It expands PM² with methods, tools and techniques for teams applying Agile and Lean practices inside a PM² project, and PM² keeps supplying the governance model, the lifecycle and the artefacts. The Business Case, Project Charter, Architecture Overview and Operational Model stay mandatory where an information system is part of the solution (p.25). The honest reason for choosing it here is the one in section 4.4: the requirements are not entirely known and the rate of change is high.
options.whyPlain: PM²-Agile does not replace any part of PM² (page 2). It adds methods and techniques for teams working in an agile way inside a PM² project. PM² still supplies the governance, the phases and the documents. The Business Case, Project Charter, Architecture Overview and Operational Model stay compulsory when the solution contains an information system (page 25). The real reason to choose agile here is the one on page 30: the requirements are not known and they change often.

options.why: The guide never sells agile on speed. It says the opposite about planning: the amount of planning effort in agile is greater than in traditionally managed projects, and its intensity is spread across the whole lifecycle (p.28). options.whyPlain: The guide never sells agile as faster. It says the opposite about planning: agile needs more planning effort than a traditional project, spread over the whole lifecycle (page 28). Promising speed to a senior committee creates a promise nobody can keep, and it hides the real reason, which is that the requirement is not known.

options.why: The guide is explicit about when the traditional route is correct: if both requestor and provider are certain the requirements specification describes the solution completely, use upfront planning (p.30). That is the CASTOR case, not this one. Fixing a scope nobody can hold still produces a specification the project then defends instead of a solution the users can use.
options.whyPlain: The guide says clearly when the traditional way is right: if both sides are certain that a written specification describes the whole solution, plan it all up front (page 30). That was true for CASTOR. It is not true here. Fixing a scope that will not hold still means the project defends a document instead of delivering a solution.

note: Guide check: sections 1 and 3.2, pp.2 and 14. PM²-Agile does not replace any part of PM². It expands PM² with methods, tools and techniques for teams applying Agile and Lean practices, tailored so that information, structures, responsibilities and artefacts stay coherent. PM² acknowledges the uncertain nature of many projects and the value of the Agile attitude, but states that certain management requirements cannot be fully satisfied by a purely Agile approach, which is why the serial phase lifecycle and the governance structure remain. The decision rule for this project sits in section 4.4 (p.30): the traditional upfront approach is correct when both sides are certain the specification describes the solution; agile is correct when the requirements are not entirely known or the rate of change is high. RASCI row: the Project Initiation Request is a PM² artefact, not a PM²-Agile one; the AGB or the Project Owner accepts it. Approver: the Appropriate Governance Body, here the Corporate Investment Board. Pages 2, 14 and 30.
notePlain: Rule: PM²-Agile does not replace any part of PM² (page 2). It adds ways of working for agile teams inside a PM² project, and keeps the information, roles and documents joined up. PM² accepts that projects are uncertain and that an agile attitude helps, but says some management needs cannot be met by a purely agile approach. That is why the four phases and the governance structure stay (page 14). The choice between the two is on page 30: plan everything up front when the specification really describes the solution; work in an agile way when the requirements are unknown or change often. The Project Initiation Request is a PM² document. The senior governance body approves it. Pages 2, 14 and 30.

note: Guide check: section 7.1, p.68. Within the Initiating phase the IT governance body proposes a minimum set of documentation: a Business Case, a Project Charter, an Architecture Overview and an Operational Model. PM²-Agile adds nothing to the Business Case or the Charter templates and refers the reader to the PM² Portal and Guide for both. Business Case: purpose is to capture the project's rationale, alignment with strategy, justification of the investment and budgetary needs; it is a living document re-examined at critical milestones. RASCI: AGB I, PSC C, PO A, BM R, UR C, SP S, PM S, PCT n.a. Approver: Project Owner accountable, with the Appropriate Governance Body informed. Project Charter: defines objectives in scope, time, cost and quality, high-level requirements, risks, constraints, milestones and deliverables, and is the baseline against which progress is measured. It may be initiated by the Business Manager but the Project Manager completes and submits it. RASCI: AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM S, UR C, SP S, PM R, PCT C. Approver: Project Steering Committee. Both rows use the eight PM² columns, not the six agile ones. The Charter's Features list is the key generator of the Work Items List (p.76). Page 68.
notePlain: Rule: in the Initiating phase, IT governance asks for four documents: Business Case, Project Charter, Architecture Overview and Operational Model (page 68). PM²-Agile changes nothing in the first two and points you to the PM² guide for them. The Business Case says why the project is worth doing, how it fits the strategy, why the money is justified, and what budget is needed. It stays alive and is checked again at important milestones. Business Manager Responsible, Project Owner Accountable. The Project Charter defines scope, time, cost and quality, plus requirements, risks, milestones and deliverables. It is the baseline for measuring progress. The Business Manager may start it, but the Project Manager completes it and submits it, and the Steering Committee approves it. Both use the eight PM² columns, not the six agile ones. The Charter's features are the main source of the Work Items List. Page 68.

note: Guide check: section 3.3.1, p.17. Projects pass through the same four PM² phases and PM²-Agile keeps them. The interfaces between phases are seldom cleanly separated and planning-type activities continue into the following phase, but the guide is explicit that project phases still exist and that a common understanding between team members and other stakeholders should be fostered. Team-level tasks are not sequential: planning, analysing, coding, testing and reviewing happen in every iteration. That is the mindset driver on p.23, be serial in the large and iterative in the small. The Architecture Overview and Operational Model are Created in Initiating (pp.70, 72), which is why they exist at this gate. The agile roles are introduced from section 6.3: Team Coordinator facilitates and coaches and hides project management concerns from the team (p.62); Product Owner continuously prioritises the Work Items List and is the single voice of the stakeholders (p.63); Architecture Owner is the team's solution architect (p.63). RASCI row: none, the Phase Exit Review Checklist has no row. Approver: nobody approves the checklist; the Project Steering Committee authorises the phase transition. Page 17.
notePlain: Rule: a PM²-Agile project keeps the four PM² phases: Initiating, Planning, Executing, Closing (page 17). The boundaries between phases are not clean, and planning work continues into the next phase. But the phases still exist, and the guide says everyone should understand them in the same way. Inside a team the work is not in sequence: planning, analysis, coding, testing and review happen in every iteration. The guide sums this up as: be serial in the large, iterative in the small (page 23). The Architecture Overview and the Operational Model are created in Initiating, so they exist at this gate. The agile roles arrive here too: the Team Coordinator facilitates and protects the team from project management work; the Product Owner keeps the Work Items List ordered and speaks for the stakeholders; the Architecture Owner is the team's architect. Nobody approves the checklist. The Steering Committee approves the move to the next phase. Page 17.

note: Guide check: sections 3.1 and 3.4, pp.13 and 22-23. PM²-Agile adopts, with modifications, the twelve principles of the Agile Manifesto. Four of them are load-bearing here: the highest priority is early and continuous delivery of valuable solutions; deliver value frequently through working solutions; simplicity, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, is essential; and agile practices should be enterprise-aware, considering IT governance, enterprise architecture and interoperability requirements, with agile teams able to collaborate with teams following other approaches. The PM²-Agile Mindsets extend the eleven PM² Mindsets with drivers including making over analysis, organise work around timeboxes not the other way around, and be as agile as needed and as agile as possible within the constraints of the organisation. Overproduction is the second Lean waste (p.5) and extra features are its usual form. RASCI row: none, principles have no artefact row. Approver: none. The priority decision belongs to the Product Owner. Pages 13 and 23.
notePlain: Rule: PM²-Agile takes the twelve agile principles and changes them slightly (page 13). Four matter here. Satisfy the client through early and continuous delivery of valuable solutions. Deliver value often through working solutions. Simplicity, the art of maximising the work not done, is essential. And agile practice must be enterprise-aware: IT governance, enterprise architecture and interoperability all count, and agile teams must work with teams that are not agile. The PM²-Agile mindsets add short rules such as making over analysis, organise work around timeboxes, and be as agile as needed and as possible inside the limits of the organisation (page 23). Producing more than is needed is the second kind of Lean waste, and extra features are the usual form of it (page 5). No document, no RASCI row and no approver here. The priority decision belongs to the Product Owner.

note: Guide check: section 7.2.1, pp.72-73, with tailoring at pp.25-26. The Development Handbook documents the selected approach for developing the information system and how the domain-specific aspect relates to the overall project level. It is an extension of the Project Handbook, aligned with its key controlling processes, policies, rules and management approach. It extends three areas of the Project Handbook: roles and responsibilities, including deviations from the standard PM²-Agile roles and the standard RASCI table; the project management plans; and the domain-specific artefacts, with tailoring recorded. The guidelines require the progress measurement to be described clearly, the requirements approach to make stories visible as the working units, and the change management process to be adjusted for stakeholder collaboration. It is a living artefact: outcomes of Iteration Retrospectives and Reviews are documented in it, and in Closing it is a point of reference for the project-end review before being archived. RASCI: BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM S — the guide's own worked example on p.66. Approver: the Project Manager is Accountable; the Business Manager is only Informed. Lifecycle: Created in Planning, Updated in Executing. Pages 72-73.

It extends three parts of the Project Handbook: roles and responsibilities, including any deviation from the standard agile roles and the standard RASCI table; the management plans; and the agile artefacts, with the tailoring written down. It is a living document: whatever a retrospective or review changes is recorded here. In Closing it is used for the project-end review and then archived. note: Guide check: sections 7.2.2 to 7.2.2.3, pp.74-80. The Development Work Plan is a container of different perspectives on what needs to be done and how the development goals will be achieved. It has two parts: the Work Items List, holding user stories, enabler stories and defects, all prioritised and estimated at some point because the list is the main driver of the project; and Schedules, at two detail levels. In the Release Plan the focus is primarily on what needs to be done and when. In an Iteration Plan the focus is on how it will be done by the team. The Development Work Plan becomes part of the Project Work Plan and must align with the project milestones defined by the Project Manager and the whole Project Core Team. It is a living artefact, kept current as information and progress arrive. RASCI: Development Work Plan BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM S (p.75). Work Items List BM S, PM A, TeCo C, PrOw R, ArOw S, ATeM S (p.76) — the only agile row where the Business Manager Supports and the Team Coordinator is Consulted. Release Plan BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM S (p.78). Iteration Plan BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw C, ArOw S, ATeM S (p.80). Approver: the Project Manager is Accountable for all four rows. Pages 74-80.
notePlain: Rule: the Development Work Plan holds three things, not one (page 74). The Work Items List holds user stories, enabler stories and defects. Everything in it is put in priority order and estimated at some point, because that list drives the project. Then there are two schedules. The Release Plan says what will be done and when. The Iteration Plan says how the team will do it. The Development Work Plan becomes part of the Project Work Plan and must fit the project milestones. It is a living document, kept up to date as work progresses. Who is who: the Team Coordinator is Responsible for the Work Plan, the Release Plan and the Iteration Plan, and the Project Manager is Accountable for all of them. The Work Items List is different: the Product Owner is Responsible, the Business Manager Supports and the Team Coordinator is only Consulted. That row is the one to remember. Pages 74 to 80.

note: Guide check: sections 7.1.3 and 7.1.4, pp.69-72. The Architecture Overview gives a high-level view of the software architecture to be developed, its major building blocks, and how the architecture contributes to all the capabilities of the system. It formally documents the critical architectural decisions and how compliance concerns such as security, data protection and anti-fraud are addressed, and where a Reference Architecture exists it documents how the system uses it. Where a well-defined architecture already exists, the artefact can be lighter and refer to it. Crucially it is a source of enablement work: it is an invaluable source of Enablers that populate the Work Items List. The Operational Model describes the operational aspect of the same architecture — infrastructure, logical and physical, deployment units, nodes and their placement, and the connections between nodes — and the guide requires alignment between the two. Balance is section 4.4 on p.32: focusing only on business items means the team struggles once the lack of architecture hits velocity; focusing only on enablers produces a robust solution with none of the functionality users expect, and the Architecture Owner helps the Product Owner find the balance. RASCI: Architecture Overview BM I, PM A, TeCo S, PrOw I, ArOw R, ATeM S (p.70). Operational Model PM A, TeCo S, PrOw I, ArOw R, ATeM S (p.71 — the row prints no BM column). Approver: the Project Manager is Accountable for both. Lifecycle: both Created in Initiating, Updated in Planning and Executing. Pages 69-72.
notePlain: Rule: the Architecture Overview gives a high-level picture of the software architecture: the main building blocks and how they support the system's capabilities (page 69). It records the critical architecture decisions, and how security, data protection and anti-fraud are handled. Where the organisation already has standard patterns, it shows how the system uses them. If a good architecture already exists, this document can be short and simply refer to it. It is also the main source of enabler work items for the Work Items List (page 70). The Operational Model describes the same architecture from the infrastructure side: deployment units, nodes, where they run, and the connections between them. The two must stay aligned. On balance, page 32 says: build only business items and the missing architecture will slow you down; build only enablers and users get nothing. The Architecture Owner helps the Product Owner find the balance. For both documents the Architecture Owner is Responsible, the Project Manager Accountable, and the Product Owner only Informed. Both are created in Initiating.

options.why: PM²-Agile recognises three ways of exposing work: exposure of individual Work Items, exposure at the end of an iteration, and a Release. Exposure at the end of the iteration is the one that supports the Iteration Review, and it covers the items deemed ready for review during that iteration (p.20). The iteration produces a product increment that brings the system one step closer to the final product (p.19), and the Review is where the Product Owner and stakeholders judge it against the goal. It is not a Release, which is a Solution Increment delivered to users as a real product.
options.whyPlain: PM²-Agile has three ways of showing work: one finished work item at a time, everything ready at the end of an iteration, and a Release. What happens at the end of an iteration supports the Iteration Review, and covers the items ready for review in that iteration (page 20). The iteration produces an increment that brings the system one step closer to the final product (page 19), and the Review is where the Product Owner and stakeholders judge it against the goal. It is not a Release, because a Release goes to users as a real product.
ref: Exposure at the end of an Iteration – This occurs at the end of the Iteration and supports the Iteration review ceremony

note: Guide check: sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.3, pp.19-21, with the ceremonies at pp.41-47. An agile iteration is a period in which the team produces a stable, potentially shippable part of the solution together with any supporting documentation or deliverables. Iterations are timeboxed: the duration is fixed and the scope of the content is actively managed to meet the schedule. Each iteration produces a product increment. PM²-Agile recognises three ways of exposing work: exposure of individual Work Items, exposure at the end of an iteration supporting the Iteration Review, and a Release, which is an agreed Solution Increment delivered to client and users as a real product, containing the Done items of several iterations. Iteration Planning is the first activity of the iteration, sized at two hours per iteration week — four hours for eight members over two weeks (p.42). The Daily Stand-up is sixty to ninety seconds per member (p.46); its RASCI on p.47 has the Project Manager merely Informed. The Iteration Goal is defined by the Product Owner and committed to by the team (p.79). RASCI: no artefact row for the gate itself; the Test Plan row is BM I, PM A, TeCo S, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM R (p.81), which is the only agile row where an Agile Team Member is Responsible. Approver: the Project Steering Committee authorises the phase transition. Pages 19-21.
notePlain: Rule: an iteration is a fixed period in which the team makes a stable, potentially shippable part of the solution, plus any documents that go with it (page 19). The length is fixed and the scope is managed to fit it. Every iteration produces an increment. There are three ways of showing work: one work item at a time, everything ready at the end of an iteration, and a Release. Only the Release goes to users as a real product, and it contains the finished items of several iterations (page 20). Iteration Planning is the first activity of the iteration: about two hours for each week of the iteration, so four hours for a team of eight on a two-week iteration (page 42). The Daily Stand-up gives each member sixty to ninety seconds (page 46), and the Project Manager is only Informed on it. The Product Owner sets the iteration goal and the team commits to it (page 79). Note the Test Plan: the Agile Team Members are Responsible for it (page 81). The Steering Committee approves the move into Executing.
